Hey everyone! I’m Arjun, an engineering student from Kerala forming a team for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Nov 14–15).
What I bring: Engineering & hardware/electronics background, strong problem-solving, technical documentation, and visual sketching/concept design. I'm big on staying organized and actually finishing what we start.

  
Beginners and experienced builders are both welcome—if you're reliable and excited to build something cool this weekend, DM me or request to join!
summary:
For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed The Silent Guardians of the Stars, an illustrated digital storytelling book that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon, Mars, and deep space.
Addressing the challenge of translating complex historical and scientific data into an engaging narrative, our project brings silent off-world artifacts—such as Apollo lunar modules, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, NEAR Shoemaker, and Pioneer 10—back to life. Rather than relying on dense technical websites or historical textbooks, the book weaves real mission facts, engineering milestones, and telemetry data into an imaginative, accessible story.
This project is vital because students often hear only about active missions; it inspires the next generation by connecting humanity's forgotten robotic explorers to the groundbreaking science that paved the way for today's achievements and tomorrow’s exploration.
details: For over half a century, humanity has sent incredible machines to the Moon, Mars, and deep space. When their missions end, probes, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments are left behind as silent monuments to human exploration. While space agencies know their histories, school-age space enthusiasts often hear only about active missions. To bridge this gap, our project—The Silent Guardians of the Stars—transforms complex historical telemetry and scientific data into an engaging, story-driven digital children’s book and interactive narrative designed for young space enthusiasts. On the Moon, our narrative explores artifacts like Surveyor 3, which landed on April 20, 1967, after bouncing like a pogo stick because reflective rocks confused its landing radar. Equipped with a surface-sampling arm that reached 5 feet and dug 7 inches deep, Surveyor 3 proved that lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand with a bearing strength of about 10 pounds per square inch—solid enough to support a human Lunar Module. We also examine the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle descent stage left behind in Mare Tranquilitatis after Armstrong and Aldrin's historic 1969 landing, alongside the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP). Later, Apollo 12 landed within 180 meters of Surveyor 3 in November 1969, allowing astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean to retrieve its camera and parts to evaluate how 2.5 years of space exposure affected metal. On Mars, the project chronicles pioneering missions such as Mars Pathfinder and its 23-pound rover, Sojourner. Using an innovative airbag landing system, Pathfinder bounced 15 times before resting in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain cut by colossal volumes of water. Viking 1 safely touched down on July 20, 1976, returning 4,500 photos and analyzing sulfur-rich soils before its communication ceased in 1982. The story also highlights twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity—which drove an astonishing 28.06 miles—alongside Phoenix, InSight, and the Ingenuity helicopter, which completed 72 historic flights in the thin Martian atmosphere. Venture deeper into space, and the museum expands to asteroids and interstellar trajectories. In February 2001, NEAR Shoemaker became the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid, touching down gently at 4 miles per hour on 433 Eros and returning data for two weeks. The Kepler Space Telescope surveyed over 500,000 stars and revealed that 20 to 50 percent of visible stars likely harbor rocky, Earth-sized planets in their habitable zones. Finally, Pioneer 10—launched in March 1972—braved the asteroid belt and Jupiter's radiation before crossing Neptune's orbit in 1983. In January 2003, it sent its final signal from 7.6 billion miles away, carrying a gold-anodized aluminum plaque as a message from Earth to the stars.
